stages.name: Beyond the cedar route
stages.desc: Lands with little or no known contact with Egypt

stages.name: Egyptian heartland
stages.desc: The Nile kingdom of the pyramid builders

stages.name: Timber & trading partner
stages.desc: Cedar, oils and gifts exchanged with Egypt

stages.name: Transit coast & frontier
stages.desc: Coasts, roads and raiding grounds between Egypt and Byblos

states.name: Cyprus
timeline: Farming villages of Chalcolithic Cyprus, outside Egypt's horizon
Newcomers of the Philia culture bring new pottery and copper-working

states.name: Israel
timeline: Walled towns such as Megiddo stand along the land and sea routes to the north
Weni's armies raid the 'sand-dwellers' and land troops by sea
Fortified towns such as Beit Yerah are abandoned; people return to villages and herding

states.name: Palestine
timeline: Walled hill-country towns such as Jericho on the inland route
Jericho's Early Bronze Age town is destroyed and left to shepherd camps

states.name: Lebanon
timeline: Byblos (Gubla, Egyptian Kebny) ships cedar from Mount Lebanon to Egypt
Vessels naming Unas are offered in the temple of the Lady of Byblos
Gifts of Pepi I reach the temple of the Lady of Byblos
Byblos is destroyed by fire; contact with Egypt lapses

states.name: Syria
timeline: Inland Syria trades with Mesopotamia; Ebla is growing into a regional power
Ebla's palace archive records wide trade; Egyptian royal gifts reach it
Ebla's Palace G is burned, probably by the kings of Akkad

states.name: Jordan
timeline: Walled towns of the Jordan valley, such as Bab edh-Dhra, live by farming and herding
Bab edh-Dhra and other walled towns are abandoned

states.name: Egypt
timeline: Sneferu rules a united Egypt from Memphis and builds pyramids at Meidum and Dahshur
Khufu's Great Pyramid is completed at Giza
Sahure's reliefs show seagoing ships returning from the Levant
Reliefs on Unas's causeway show starving people
Pepi II begins one of the longest reigns in history
After Pepi II, short reigns, failing floods and powerful governors break the Old Kingdom apart

states.name: N. Cyprus
timeline: Farming villages of Chalcolithic Cyprus, outside Egypt's horizon
Philia-culture settlers arrive on the north coast

events.title: Forty cedar ships
events.text: The royal annal on the Palermo Stone records that forty ships filled with cedar wood came to Sneferu.

events.title: Cedars of Lebanon
events.text: Woodcutters fell cedars on Mount Lebanon and drag the logs down to the coast at Byblos.

events.title: Lady of Byblos
events.text: Byblos honours its goddess Baalat Gebal, whom Egyptians will identify with their own Hathor.

events.title: Cedar palace doors
events.text: The same annal records doors of cedar made for Sneferu's palace, and ships one hundred cubits long.

events.title: Red Pyramid
events.text: Sneferu completes his third pyramid at Dahshur, the first true smooth-sided pyramid.

events.title: Wadi Maghara
events.text: Old Kingdom expeditions mine turquoise and copper in Sinai and carve the kings' names on the rocks.

events.title: Wadi al-Jarf harbour
events.text: Khufu's crews use a harbour on the Red Sea, the oldest known, to cross to Sinai.

events.title: Khufu's boat buried
events.text: A royal boat of Lebanese cedar is dismantled and sealed in a pit beside the Great Pyramid.

events.title: Merer's logbook
events.text: Inspector Merer's crew ships white limestone from Tura to Giza; his papyri were found at Wadi al-Jarf in 2013.

events.title: Great Pyramid
events.text: Khufu's pyramid at Giza is completed, the largest of all Egypt's pyramids.

events.title: Khafre's pyramid
events.text: Khafre builds the second pyramid of Giza; a lid bearing his name will later reach Ebla.

events.title: Megiddo's temples
events.text: Megiddo, guarding the inland route north, builds monumental temples on its sacred area.

events.title: Temple en L
events.text: Byblos's great 'L-shaped' temple stands inside the city walls on its headland.

events.title: Sahure's sea-ships
events.text: Reliefs at Abusir show Sahure's seagoing ships returning with Asiatic families and Syrian bears.

events.title: Ayn Sukhna harbour
events.text: A second Red Sea harbour serves Fifth Dynasty expeditions to the Sinai mines.

events.title: Ebla's archives
events.text: The palace of Ebla keeps thousands of clay tablets on textiles, metals and diplomacy.

events.title: Philia culture
events.text: Newcomers bring new pottery and copper-working to Cyprus, still beyond Egypt's horizon.

events.title: Unas famine relief
events.text: Reliefs on the causeway of Unas at Saqqara show emaciated, starving people.

events.title: Unas at Byblos
events.text: Stone vessels carved with the name of Unas are offered in the temple of the Lady of Byblos.

events.title: Pyramid Texts
events.text: Unas's burial chamber carries the first Pyramid Texts, spells for the king's afterlife.

events.title: Teti at Byblos
events.text: Vessels naming Teti, first king of the Sixth Dynasty, join the gifts at Byblos.

events.title: Pepi I at Byblos
events.text: An alabaster vessel names Pepi I as beloved of Hathor; many of his gifts reach Byblos.

events.title: Gifts at Ebla
events.text: Egyptian stone vessels naming Khafre and Pepi I reach the palace of Ebla.

events.title: Weni's campaigns
events.text: The official Weni leads five campaigns against the 'sand-dwellers', once landing troops by sea.

events.title: Ebla burned
events.text: Palace G at Ebla is burned, probably by Sargon or Naram-Sin of Akkad; the fire bakes its tablets.

events.title: Jericho falls
events.text: Jericho's Early Bronze Age walls are destroyed by fire; only shepherd camps follow.

events.title: Bab edh-Dhra emptied
events.text: The walled town by the Dead Sea is abandoned, like many towns of the southern Levant.

events.title: Eleven voyages
events.text: At Aswan, the official Khnumhotep records sailing eleven times to Byblos and to Punt.

events.title: Beit Yerah abandoned
events.text: The great walled town on the Sea of Galilee is deserted.

events.title: Pepi II crowned
events.text: Pepi II takes the throne as a child; tradition gives him a reign of over ninety years.

events.title: Harkhuf's letter
events.text: The boy king writes to his expedition leader Harkhuf, eager to see a dancer from the far south.

events.title: Pepi II at Byblos
events.text: Vessels naming Pepi II are the last Old Kingdom royal gifts found at Byblos.

events.title: Rich governors
events.text: Provincial governors build grand tombs of their own and rule their nomes like princes.

events.title: Failing floods
events.text: A drier climate weakens the Nile floods; later governors in the south boast of feeding their people in famine.

events.title: Old Kingdom falls
events.text: After Pepi II, short reigns follow at Memphis and the unified kingdom breaks apart.

events.title: Byblos burned
events.text: Byblos is destroyed by fire, by invaders or in the turmoil of the age; the date is debated.

events.title: No ships to Byblos
events.text: Centuries later, an Egyptian poem laments that no one now sails north to Byblos for cedar.

events.title: Cedar forests quiet
events.text: With Byblos in ruins, the cedar trade with Egypt lapses until the Middle Kingdom.

Regions are today's boundaries, and a whole country stands for the few ancient sites that tell its story, so Egypt dominates the shares. A simplification: dates follow conventional Old Kingdom chronology and are approximate by several decades.
